659.title: Look to others (Philippians 1:27–2:4)
659.hook: do nothing out of selfish ambition; look to others' interests
659.howItsDone: Some Christian communities take Philippians 2:3–4 as a rule for their life together, and it is often read when churches, families or teams are working through conflict.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a man in chains wrote to live is Christ, and to die is gain, and your line was a strait betwixt two.

Being Romans. That's how the crowd at Philippi puts it in the book of Acts, dragging Paul before the magistrates: these men teach customs that aren't lawful for us to keep, being Romans. Acts calls the city a colony, a piece of Rome set down in Macedonia. So when Paul writes to the church in Philippi about how to live, he reaches for a word every one of them knew: the word for being a citizen.

The King James Bible says: "Only let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel of Christ." Conversation, in old English, meant your whole way of life, not just talk. But Paul's Greek word is politeuesthe: live as citizens worthy of the good news. Later in the letter he'll say their real citizenship is in heaven. You know how to be Roman; now be citizens of something else, together. Then he asks for something hard, and asks it warmly. If there's any comfort in Christ, any fellowship of the Spirit, any tenderness, then "Fulfil ye my joy, that ye be likeminded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind." Make my joy complete by getting along. It seems the Philippians had some friction; later he names two women who need to agree. Then the heart of it: "Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves." Vainglory is empty glory: doing things to look good. Lowliness of mind is humility. Some readers point out that in ordinary Greek, lowly could mean servile, beneath you, and Paul turns it into something to aim for. Then: "Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others." Notice the small word also. Paul doesn't say ignore your own needs. He says don't stop at them. It's a picture of a community where everyone quietly watches out for someone else, and someone else watches out for them. Tomorrow, Paul gives the reason: the pattern of Christ himself.
screen: `MAKE MY JOY COMPLETE: BE OF ONE MIND.`
`NO EMPTY GLORY; HUMILITY AS A VIRTUE.`
then, large: `LOOK NOT EVERY MAN ON HIS OWN THINGS.`

segments.voice: Think of the people you'll be around today and pick one. What do they need that you could notice: the last good parking spot, the chance to finish their story, credit for their idea, the bigger slice? Choose one way to put their interest ahead of yours without making a show of it, and if you pray, ask for eyes to see what others need.
Vainglory. Paul's word for empty glory, doing things to look good: he asks a proud Roman colony to let humility and others' needs come first instead.
Your line: others first. Your own things, and also the things of others. See you tomorrow.

660.title: He emptied himself (Philippians 2:5–11)
660.hook: an early hymn: he took the form of a servant, humbled himself to death
660.carry: all the way down, for others
660.howItsDone: Many churches read Philippians 2:5–11 on Palm Sunday, and in some traditions people bow their heads at the name of Jesus, a custom drawn from this hymn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Roman colony told to live as citizens of something else, and your line was others first.

In the middle of a letter from prison, Paul's writing suddenly changes rhythm. The sentences start to balance, line against line, like poetry. Many scholars think Paul is quoting a hymn here, something the earliest Christians already sang, within a few decades of the crucifixion. If they're right, these six verses are among the oldest words about Jesus we have. Some think Paul wrote them himself. Either way, the shape is unmistakable: a song that goes all the way down, and then all the way up.
screen: `ALL THE WAY DOWN, ALL THE WAY UP.`

segments.voice: It begins: "Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus." Then the descent. In the King James Bible: "Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men." The Greek is shorter and sharper: ekenosen, he emptied himself. From that verb comes today's word, kenosis, self-emptying. He didn't treat equality with God as something to grab or cling to. He let go. Then the steps keep going down: a servant, a human being. "he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross." The cross was the death Rome used for slaves and rebels. Then the turn. "Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him." All the way up: "That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow," in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord. Those lines echo the prophet Isaiah, where God says every knee will bow to him; the hymn hears that promise fulfilled in Jesus. What exactly did he empty himself of? Christians have asked that for centuries. Most churches teach that he didn't stop being God, but set aside the privileges, taking on our limits, our hunger, our death. Some modern theologians have pushed the idea further. All agree on the direction: down, for others. And that's Paul's point for the Philippians. Look to others, because this is the mind of Christ.
screen: `DOWN TO THE DEATH OF THE CROSS.`

segments.voice: Think of something that needs doing that nobody wants to do and nobody will thank you for: a neighbor's trash cans, listening to someone everyone else avoids. Notice the small voice that says that's not my job, and picture yourself doing it anyway, quietly, the way a servant would. If you pray, you can pray the hymn's first line: let this mind be in me.
Kenosis. Greek for self-emptying: the hymn's picture of Christ letting go of his rights and going all the way down, for others.
Your line: all the way down, for others. That's the shape of the song. Day six hundred sixty, done.

661.title: Shine like stars (Philippians 2:12–18)
661.hook: do everything without grumbling, shining like stars
661.howItsDone: Some Christians take on a fast from complaining for a day or a season, especially in Lent, and some families and youth groups use Philippians 2:14–15 for it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kenosis: a hymn that went all the way down, and your line was all the way down, for others.

Count your complaints for one morning. Not the big ones. The coffee's cold. The traffic. The meeting that could've been an email. The weather, which you can't change and mention anyway. It's easy to lose count before lunch. Grumbling is a kind of background noise of being human. So it's a little startling that, right after the hymn of Christ emptying himself, Paul comes down to earth and says: do everything without grumbling.

First, a famous and much-argued line. In the King James Bible: "work out your own salvation with fear and trembling." And immediately: "For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure." You work it out, because God is working in you. Christians balance those two halves differently. Catholic and Orthodox Christians often stress cooperation with grace. Many Protestants stress that the working out flows from a salvation already given. Read either way, the two sentences belong together. Then the practical part: "Do all things without murmurings and disputings." Some readers hear an echo of Israel in the wilderness, where the King James uses the same word, murmur, for complaints about the food and the water on the long road out of Egypt. If the echo is meant, Paul is reaching for a story his own scriptures already told about how hard trust is on a long road. Then the picture: "That ye may be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world." Crooked and perverse echoes the song of Moses in Deuteronomy. And the word for lights is phosteres, the word the old Greek translation of Genesis uses for the lights God set in the sky: sun, moon and stars. So a small church in a Roman town can be like stars in a dark sky. Not by being loud, but by not grumbling, by holding forth the word of life. And a quiet line about himself: if my life is poured out like an offering, I'm glad. I rejoice with you all.
screen: `WORK IT OUT, FOR GOD IS AT WORK IN YOU.`
then, large: `AMONG WHOM YE SHINE AS LIGHTS IN THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Notice a complaint already forming about today, name it, and let it go on the out-breath; then do the same with the next one. Picture the moments you're most likely to grumble, the commute, a certain coworker, the dinner dishes, and picture meeting each with quiet instead, or even something kind. If you pray, you can ask for help with the hardest one.
Phosteres. Greek for lights, the word Genesis uses for the sun, moon and stars: Paul's picture for a small church, shining without grumbling in a dark sky.
Your line: shine as lights. Stars don't shout. That's day six hundred sixty-one.

662.title: Timothy and Epaphroditus (Philippians 2:19–30)
662.hook: two friends honored: one who cares, one who nearly died serving
662.howItsDone: Many churches remember helpers by name in their prayers and announcements, and some traditions honor Timothy and other companions of Paul with feast days in the church calendar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a small church told to shine like stars, and your line was shine as lights.

At the end of a film the credits roll: the grip, the caterer, the person who drove the van. Plenty of people are out the door before they finish. A few lines after the great hymn of Christ emptied and lifted up, Paul's letter does something that looks almost ordinary. Travel plans. Two names. A man who has served beside him like a son, and a man from Philippi itself who brought a gift and nearly died delivering it. The letter stops to roll the credits, and Paul reads them out slowly.

First, Timothy. Paul is in chains, and he hopes to send Timothy to Philippi soon. In the King James Bible: "For I have no man likeminded, who will naturally care for your state." Naturally. Not because he's told to. Timothy simply cares. And a family picture: "as a son with the father, he hath served with me in the gospel." Acts says Timothy's mother was a Jewish believer and his father Greek, and that Paul took him along on his travels. Then, Epaphroditus. Everything we know about him is in this letter. The church at Philippi sent him to carry their gift to Paul in prison and to stay and help. Somewhere along the way he fell ill. "For indeed he was sick nigh unto death: but God had mercy on him; and not on him only, but on me also, lest I should have sorrow upon sorrow." Paul doesn't pretend. He would have grieved. And a tender detail: Epaphroditus is homesick and heavy-hearted, not about his illness, but because the people back home heard he was ill, and he hates to think of them worrying. So Paul sends him home: "Receive him therefore in the Lord with all gladness; and hold such in reputation." Modern versions say honor. The courier. The helper. The one who almost didn't make it back. In a letter about Christ lowering himself, Paul shows what that looks like in two ordinary lives, and asks the church to lift them up.
screen: then, large: `RECEIVE HIM WITH ALL GLADNESS.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who helps and is rarely thanked out loud: the person who covers the shift, the neighbor who takes in the packages, the relative who always drives. Remember one specific thing they did, and imagine saying it by name in front of others, short and true, the way Paul did in a letter read aloud to a whole church. If you pray, you can give thanks for them by name.
Epaphroditus. The Philippians' courier who nearly died bringing their gift to Paul in prison, and whom Paul sends home asking the church to hold him in honor.
Your line: hold such in honor. The helpers belong in the story too. Until tomorrow.

663.title: Counting it loss (Philippians 3:1–11)
663.hook: everything Paul was proud of, he counts as loss compared with knowing Christ
663.howItsDone: Many Christians read Philippians 3 when thinking about pride and identity, and some churches use verses 7 to 11 in Lent as a reflection on what to set aside.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Timothy and Epaphroditus, two helpers named in a letter, and your line was hold such in honor.

A résumé, printed on the good paper. Born into the right family. The best teachers. A record nobody can fault. Then the owner takes a red pen and writes across the whole page: loss. Not shredding it. Not lying about it. Just marking it down, as if the numbers had been in the wrong column all along. That's close to what Paul does in the third chapter of Philippians. He lays out every credential he had, then moves the whole list to the other side of the ledger.

Here's the list, in the King James Bible: "Circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, an Hebrew of the Hebrews; as touching the law, a Pharisee." He kept the law of his people with great zeal, and says that by its measure of righteousness he was blameless. He isn't mocking any of it. These are real goods: an honored family, a faithful upbringing, a serious life. "But what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ." It's bookkeeping language: gain and loss. Then he goes further: "I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord." All things. And he uses a rough word for them, one that means refuse, the scraps you throw out. Older English Bibles put it bluntly as dung. Why so strong? Because what he wants now is not a record but a person: "That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings." Know, here, is not knowing about. It's the way you know a friend. Christians read this passage in different ways. Some hear a conversion from one way of standing before God to another. Others stress that Paul never stops being a Jew, and that what he counts as loss is his own standing, his pride, not the Torah or his people. Both readings see the turn: the things that once defined him no longer get to.
screen: then, large: `I COUNT ALL THINGS BUT LOSS.`

segments.voice: Name something you're proud of that quietly runs your life: a title, a grade, being the one who's always right, or always busy, or always fine. It may be a real good, as Paul's were, so don't throw it away; just picture writing it on a card and moving it out of the center, and notice what's left in the middle. If you pray, you can hand it to God and leave the card there.
Pharisee. Paul's own credential before his bookkeeping turn: a label he moved, with everything else he had, into the loss column, next to knowing Christ.
Your line: all else is loss. A record, traded for a person. That's day six hundred sixty-three.

664.title: Press on (Philippians 3:12–21)
664.hook: forgetting what lies behind, straining forward
664.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Philippians 3:13–14 at new beginnings, such as a new year, a graduation or a recovery.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a whole résumé moved into the loss column, and your line was all else is loss.

Watch the last fifty meters of a race. Nobody in the lead looks back. Coaches drill it: turn your head to see who's behind you, and you lose a step. The runners lean forward, chest out, reaching for a line on the ground. Paul has just told the Philippians that everything behind him is loss. Now he faces the other way, and reaches for the language of the stadium: a track, a line, a prize.

He starts with an admission. Paul, the great apostle, says he hasn't arrived. In the King James Bible: "Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended." Not yet. I haven't got hold of it. Then the famous lines: "this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus." Every phrase is a runner. Forgetting what's behind. Reaching forth, the body leaning out. The mark, the goal at the end of the track. The prize. The verb for press is worth a second look. In Greek it's a word for chasing, pursuing hard. A few verses earlier, Paul used the very same word about his past: he had been zealous, persecuting the church. The same energy that once hunted Christians now runs toward Christ. Paul doesn't become a calmer man. He points the same drive in a new direction. And forgetting isn't amnesia. He remembers his past well enough to write it down a few verses earlier. He means it no longer steers: not his old credentials, not his old wrongs. Then he widens the picture: "For our conversation is in heaven." You live here, he says, but your city is somewhere else. So you run.
screen: then, large: `I PRESS TOWARD THE MARK.`

segments.voice: Think of something you keep replaying, a failure, an old win, a conversation you can't stop rewriting, and notice how much attention it still takes. Then gently turn your head the other way: what's one small thing in front of you that you've put off while you looked back, a call, a page, an apology, a first lap? Picture taking the first step toward it, just one, and if you pray, ask for help to run.
Press on. Paul's runner's word: chase hard toward the goal, the same verb he once used for persecuting, now aimed forward.
Your line: forgetting what's behind, reaching forth. The race isn't over yet. See you on the track tomorrow.

665.title: Help these women (Philippians 4:1–3)
665.hook: Euodia and Syntyche, co-workers, are asked to agree
665.howItsDone: Many churches ask a trusted third person, a pastor, elder or friend, to help members reconcile, and some read Philippians 4:2–3 when teaching about peacemaking in the congregation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a runner pressing toward the mark, and your line was forgetting what's behind, reaching forth.

Two names, and that's almost all we know: Euodia and Syntyche. Paul's letter will be read aloud to the whole church at Philippi, and in the middle of it he names two women who aren't getting along. We don't know what the quarrel was about. Money, a meeting, a hurt word, a plan for the church. The letter never says, and it's honest to leave it there. What we do know is how Paul handles it. He doesn't take a side. He doesn't send a rebuke. He asks for help.

First he speaks to the whole church with real warmth: they are, in the King James Bible, "my joy and crown." Then: "I beseech Euodias, and beseech Syntyche, that they be of the same mind in the Lord." He says beseech twice, once to each woman. Neither is named first as the problem. And same mind is a phrase from all through this letter: be likeminded, let this mind be in you. It doesn't mean agreeing on every detail. It means facing the same direction. Then he turns to someone else: "And I intreat thee also, true yokefellow, help those women which laboured with me in the gospel." Who is the yokefellow? Nobody knows. Some think it's a friend Paul doesn't name. Some think Syzygos, Greek for yokefellow, was the man's actual name. Either way, a third person is asked to help two people find their way back. And look how Paul describes these women: not as troublemakers, but as co-workers who labored with him in the gospel, along with Clement and the rest, "whose names are in the book of life." Their quarrel doesn't cancel their work. Philippi's church began, Acts says, with women at a place of prayer by a river, and Lydia opening her home. Women were there from the start. This week has walked through Philippians: look to others, he emptied himself, shine like stars, two helpers honored, counting it loss, press on, and now two co-workers asked to agree.
screen: `CO-WORKERS, NAMES IN THE BOOK OF LIFE.`
then, large: `BE OF THE SAME MIND IN THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Think of two people you know who have drifted apart or fallen out, friends, siblings, coworkers, and don't decide who's right; Paul didn't. Picture each of them and remember one good thing each has done, then ask whether there's a small way to help without taking sides, even just by not feeding the quarrel. If you pray, you can hold both of them before God by name.
Syzygos. Greek for yokefellow, one who pulls in the same yoke, maybe even the man's own name: Paul's friend, asked to help Euodia and Syntyche find the same mind again.
Your line: be of one mind. Facing the same direction, not agreeing on everything. A week of Philippians, done.

chat.says: Two women in Paul's church were quarreling. Whose side did he take?
options: Neither. He begged each by name to be of one mind, and asked a friend to help.
Euodia's, because he named her first and called the other one stubborn.
Neither, so he told the church to put them both out until they agreed.
